label: Four definitions of economics
text: Adam Smith (1776): the nature and causes of the wealth of nations. Alfred Marshall (1890): a study of man in the ordinary business of life and the material requisites of well-being. Lionel Robbins (1932): human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses. Paul Samuelson (1948): how societies use scarce resources to produce valuable commodities and distribute them among different people.

label: Managerial economics questions
text: What price should a firm charge for its product? How much output should be produced? How many workers should be hired?

label: Accounting cost and opportunity cost examples
text: Accounting costs: wages, rent, electricity, raw materials. Opportunity cost: owner's time, foregone salary, own building used for business.

label: Factors that affect profitability
text: A star labelled Sustainable Industry Profits with five boxes pointing at it: Entry, Power of Input Suppliers, Power of Buyers, Industry Rivalry, and Substitutes & Complements.

label: Sales representative incentive
text: Firm's goal: increase sales. Employee's incentive: earn a sales commission. Result: higher effort, higher sales, higher earnings for the employee and higher profits for the firm.

label: ₹10,000 today or in a year
text: Would you prefer ₹10,000 today or ₹10,000 one year from now? The opportunity cost of waiting a year is the interest foregone that could be earned from investing ₹10,000 today.

label: Advertising intensity case
text: Three advertising intensities for a new model, discounted at 10%: High $303.31M, Low $256.76M, Moderate $214.39M. High maximizes the present value even though it has the lowest profits in Years 1-2.

label: $5,000 machine
text: Cost $5000, $2000 a year for 3 years at 7%: PV = $5,248.63, NPV = 5,248.63 - 5000 = $248.63. NPV > 0, so the firm should buy the machine.

label: Break-room refrigerator
text: Energy-efficient model at $550 saving $28 at the end of each of the next 5 years, or a standard model at $420 with no savings; opportunity cost of funds 5 percent. Which should you buy?

label: Deferred perpetuity endowment
text: An endowment pays $800 per year forever, with the first payment at the end of Year 5, at an interest rate of 6%. What is its present value today?

label: Firm with constant $50,000 profits
text: Profits of $50,000 paid out as dividends forever, first paid at the end of this year, i = 10%: PV(firm) = 0 + 50,000 / 0.10 = $500,000.

label: Software company valuation scenarios
text: Current profits $3.2 billion (not yet paid), interest rate 9 percent; value the firm if profits grow at 11%, 4%, 0%, or decline at 4% a year.

label: Thinking at the margin questions
text: Should the firm produce one more unit of a product? Should it hire one more worker? Should it spend ₹10,000 more on advertising? Answer: only if the additional benefit exceeds the additional cost.

label: Discrete and continuous decision examples
text: Discrete: hire one more worker, open another store. Continuous: set the selling price, decide advertising expenditure.

label: MR and MC table (outputs 0 to 6)
text: TR rises by 50 per unit (0 to 300) while TC goes 20, 40, 70, 110, 160, 220, 290. MC rises 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, so MR = MC = 50 at output 4.

label: Whole-units practice schedule
text: Q from 0 to 6 with TR 0, 90, 170, 240, 300, 350, 390 and TC 0, 50, 90, 140, 200, 270, 350. Which quantity maximizes profit?

label: TR = 50Q - Q², TC = 10Q
text: Profit 50Q - Q² - 10Q; MR = MC gives Q = 20; second order condition -2 < 0; profit = 50 * 20 - 20 * 20 - 10 * 20 = $400.

label: Monopolist practice question
text: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 - 2Q and total cost TC = 50 + 10Q + 3Q². Find the profit-maximizing quantity, price and profit.

label: Marshall: utility in Utils
text: Next to the line that utility can not be measured, the slide gives Marshall's view: utility can be measured in Utils.

label: Warehouse shirt vs store shelf shirt
text: A shirt sitting in a warehouse and a shirt on a store shelf are physically identical. Why is one worth more to you?

label: T-shirt journey from Tiruppur to Delhi
text: Raw cotton at a Tiruppur mill is stitched into a T-shirt (form utility), shipped to a Delhi shelf (place utility), and stored until summer to be sold in season (time utility).

label: Whole chicken, chicken parts, cooked chicken
text: Form utility: a product available as whole chicken, chicken parts or cooked chicken; each step adds value.

label: Home delivery
text: Place utility: the place where a product is available; convenience, such as home delivery.

label: Diminishing marginal utility table
text: Units 1 to 6. Total utility: 30, 50, 60, 60, 50, 45. Marginal utility: 30, 20, 10, 0, -10, -5.

label: Total utility and marginal utility graph
text: The red total utility line rises, peaks at unit 4 and then falls; the blue marginal utility line slopes down and crosses zero between units 4 and 5.

label: ₹100 on samosas or tea
text: You have ₹100 to spend this evening on samosas or on tea. How do you decide what quantities of each to consume?

label: Samosa and tea MU/Px table
text: Marginal utility of samosa 100, 80, 60, 40, 20, 10 with MU/Px (samosa = ₹10) 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 1. Marginal utility of tea 120, 100, 80, 60, 40, 20 with MU/Px (tea = ₹20) 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Equal MU/Px values are shaded the same colour.

label: Ola fare on a rainy Friday night
text: 9 PM, normal: ₹180. 9 PM, raining: ₹540. Why does your Ola cost 3x on a rainy Friday night? Ola recalculates price in real time based on the ratio of ride requests to available drivers nearby. The deck asks: what changed, demand or supply?

label: Change in quantity demanded: A to B
text: On demand curve D0, point A is at a price of 10 and quantity 4; point B is at a price of 6 and quantity 7. A to B: increase in quantity demanded.

label: Inverse demand example
text: Demand function Qxd = 10 - 2Px; inverse demand function Px = 5 - 0.5Qxd.

label: Change in demand: D0 to D1
text: At a price of 6, quantity demanded is 7 on D0 and 13 on D1. D0 to D1: increase in demand.

label: Demand for good X question
text: Qxd = 140 - 5Px + 4Py - 6Pz + 0.01M with Py = ₹50, Pz = ₹40 and average income M = ₹30,000. Is Y a substitute or complement? Is Z? Is X normal or inferior? Find the inverse demand function, graph it, and find units purchased when Px = ₹40.

label: A great deal and a lousy deal
text: Great deal: That company offers a lot of bang for the buck! Dell provides good value. Total value greatly exceeds total amount paid, so consumer surplus is large. Lousy deal: That car dealer drives a hard bargain! I almost decided not to buy it! They tried to squeeze the very last cent from me! Total amount paid is close to total value, so consumer surplus is low.

label: Consumer surplus: the discrete case
text: Demand line D from a price of 10 to a quantity of 5; price 2, four units bought. Consumer surplus = (8-2) + (6-2) + (4-2) = $12.

label: Consumer surplus: the continuous case
text: Value of 4 units = $24. Expenditure on 4 units = $2 x 4 = $8. Consumer surplus = $24 - $8 = $16.

label: Consumer surplus practice question
text: Inverse demand Px = 80 - 0.2Qd; inverse supply Px = 10 + 0.2Qs. Find consumer surplus at the market equilibrium (P = ₹45), at Px = ₹35 and at Px = ₹60, and say what happens to consumer surplus as the price falls.

label: Change in quantity supplied: A to B
text: On supply curve S0, point A is at a price of 10 and quantity 5; point B is at a price of 20 and quantity 10. A to B: increase in quantity supplied.

label: Inverse supply example
text: Supply function Qxs = 10 + 2Px; the slide prints the inverse supply function as Px = 5 + 0.5Qxs.

label: Change in supply: S0 to S1
text: At a price of 8, quantity supplied is 5 on S0 and 7 on S1. At a quantity of 5, the price is 8 on S0 and 6 on S1. S0 to S1: increase in supply.

label: Supply of product X question
text: Qxs = 40 + 5Px - 3Pz, where Pz is the price of a key input. Find output when Px = ₹100 and Pz = ₹30, and when Px = ₹20 and Pz = ₹30. With Pz = ₹30, find the reduced supply function and the inverse supply function, and graph it.

label: If price is too low: shortage
text: Demand D and supply S cross at a price of 7. At a price of 5, quantity supplied is 6 and quantity demanded is 12: Shortage 12 - 6 = 6. Arrows point up both curves toward the crossing point.

label: If price is too high: surplus
text: Demand D and supply S cross at a price of 7 and a quantity of 8. At a price of 9, quantity demanded is 6 and quantity supplied is 14: Surplus 14 - 6 = 8. Arrows point down both curves toward the crossing point.

label: Equilibrium question for good X
text: Qxd = 400 - 5Px and Qxs = -50 + 5Px. Find the equilibrium price and quantity and show the equilibrium graphically.

label: Producer surplus practice question
text: Inverse demand Px = 80 - 0.2Qd; inverse supply Px = 10 + 0.2Qs. Find producer surplus at the market equilibrium (P = ₹45) and at Px = ₹50 (a price floor scenario), and say what happens to producer surplus as the price rises.

label: Price ceiling examples
text: National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) fixing prices of stents and other price saving drugs; price caps on surge pricing for Uber / Ola.

label: Price floor examples
text: Minimum wage; agricultural price supports.

label: Price ceiling of ₹40 question
text: Qxd = 400 - 5Px; Qxs = -50 + 5Px. With a price ceiling of ₹40, find Qxd, Qxs, the magnitude of the shortage, and the full economic price paid by consumers.

label: Price floor of ₹50 question
text: Qxd = 400 - 5Px; Qxs = -50 + 5Px. With a price floor of ₹50, find Qxd, Qxs, the magnitude of the surplus, and the cost to the government if it buys the surplus.

label: Rice price and export headlines
text: Two news headlines: India export rice prices edge up on demand; global rates rise amid Middle East tensions (Last Updated: Apr 09, 2026). India's rice exports to rise over 10% in FY26 on robust global demand; in the 2024-25 fiscal, India exported 20.1 million tonnes of rice valued at $12.95 billion, reaching more than 172 countries.

label: Fall in PC component prices
text: The WSJ reports that the prices of PC components are expected to fall by 5-8 percent over the next six months. Scenario 1: you manage a small firm that manufactures PCs. Scenario 2: you manage a small software company.

label: PC market after component prices fall
text: Supply shifts right from S to S*; the equilibrium price of PCs falls from P0 to P* and the quantity rises from Q0 to Q*.

label: Action plan for a small PC maker
text: Inventories: sell down stock built with expensive components faster; time new production to align with cheaper components. Human resources: staff up production to capture higher volume? Marketing: lead with price cuts, or protect margin by bundling features/software? Quantitative estimates: how much to cut price (3%? 8%?) and how much more to order need demand elasticity, size of cost shift and competitor pass-through.

label: Software market after PC prices fall
text: Demand for software shifts right from D to D*; supply S stays put. The price of software rises from P0 to P1 and the quantity rises from Q0 to Q1.

label: Action plan for a software maker
text: Inventories: ramp up cloud infrastructure ahead of the expected demand surge. Human resources: staff up customer support and sales before the PC price drop fully plays out. Marketing: value-based messaging rather than discounting; time a launch to the PC upgrade cycle, since new PC buyers are a captive audience. Estimates: cross-price elasticity between PCs and software, and how much of the PC price drop reaches consumers versus PC makers' margins.
